title: LiteSearch-VL: Small Multimodal Search Agents viaTrajectory Distillation and Synthetic Step-DPO

paper.title: LiteSearch-VL: Small Multimodal Search Agents via Trajectory Distillation and Synthetic Step-DPO
paper.abstract: Abstract Multimodal search agents answer visual questions by interleaving image understanding, web retrieval, tool use, and evidence synthesis. Strong systems exist, but in two expensive regimes: proprietary frontier models such as GPT-5 and Gemini, or large open vision-language backbones trained with substantial agentic data and reinforcement learning. We ask a different question: when released agent trajectories are distilled into much smaller backbones under a single-node budget, what is actually transferred? We study this with LiteSearch-VL, a low-compute recipe for Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B that uses only released OpenSearch-VL trajectories, parameter-efficient LoRA adapters, and synthetic step-level preferences: DPO on GPT-5-generated hard negatives targeting five local failure modes ( premature answer, wrong tool, weak query, repeated query, ignored image ). Across 12,400 GPT-5-judged rollouts on SimpleVQA, FVQA, LiveVQA, and VDR-Bench-testmini, the dominant effect is behavioral rather than a uniform accuracy lift: full-trajectory supervised fine-tuning transfers the agent contract , taking the 2B model from almost never emitting a usable answer (1,237/1,240 no_answer rollouts) to 28.4% macro Pass@1, matching or slightly exceeding the off-the-shelf 4B base (25.6%). Synthetic preference learning and compact tool distillation act as refinements rather than phase transitions (best 4B configuration: 30.8% macro Pass@1). Finally, a controlled VDR step-budget ablation shows that extra search turns convert abstentions into wrong_entity errors rather than correct answers, identifying answer verification, not search depth, as the next bottleneck for small multimodal agents.

Finally, a controlled VDR step-budget ablation shows that extra search turns convert abstentions into wrong_entity errors rather than correct answers, identifying answer verification, not search depth, as the next bottleneck for small multimodal agents. 1 Introduction Knowledge-intensive visual questions often cannot be answered from the image alone: a model may need to identify an entity in the scene, search for external evidence, inspect a crop or an OCR region, and decide when the accumulated evidence is sufficient to commit to a final answer. This has motivated multimodal search agents that interleave reasoning with retrieval and image-processing tools rather than producing a single direct response [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . The most capable systems, however, are expensive to reproduce: they either depend on proprietary frontier models such as GPT-5 [ 4 ] and Gemini [ 5 ] , or train large open VLM backbones with long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning. OpenSearch-VL [ 3 ] changed the data landscape by releasing a 36K corpus of tool-interleaved teacher trajectories, an 8K RL prompt set, and a detailed seven-tool environment, but its strongest models are trained in a substantially larger regime than many research groups can access (agentic SFT on 256 H20 GPUs, then multi-turn GRPO on 64 H20 GPUs). This raises a separate question from frontier performance: what exactly do released multimodal search trajectories teach small VLMs? Do they transfer factual search competence, or do they first teach the more basic agent contract—how to format tool calls, use image handles, integrate observations, and stop searching with a final answer? We study this question in a deliberately constrained setting: starting from Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B, we train only LoRA adapters (vision tower frozen, multimodal projector trainable) on the released SearchVL-SFT-36k trajectories, construct a compact three-tool distilled variant to probe tool-surface complexity, and build synthetic step-level DPO pairs by asking GPT-5 to generate plausible local mistakes at teacher decision points. Our evaluation covers ten model cells across four short-answer, knowledge-intensive benchmarks: SimpleVQA, FVQA, LiveVQA, and VDR-Bench-testmini. The clearest result is that SFT transfers the agent contract : the 2B base model emits no usable final answer on 1,237 of 1,240 questions (0.1% macro Pass@1), while after one epoch of full-trajectory SFT the same backbone reaches 28.4% macro Pass@1 and matches the 4B base on the three easier benchmarks. This is not simply a scaling result: the 4B base already follows the contract on many questions, so its SFT gain is much smaller. The later stages are more diagnostic than transformative: synthetic step-level DPO improves the macro average by +1.0 points on 2B and +1.7 points on 4B, with the largest localized gain on FVQA but a non-uniform effect across domains; the compact three-tool interface reduces performance at 2B, is nearly cost-free at 4B on average, and strongest on FVQA; and increasing the VDR step budget from 5 to 8 reduces no_answer substantially but barely changes Pass@1—the recovered rollouts mostly become wrong_entity , pointing at verification, not search depth, as the remaining bottleneck. Our contributions are: • A low-compute recipe for 2B/4B multimodal search agents from released trajectories on one eight-GPU node. • Full-trajectory SFT as a qualitative transition (2B no_answer 1,237 → \to 514; Pass@1 0.1% → \to 28.4%). • Synthetic step-level DPO and compact tool distillation evaluated as refinements, not phase transitions. • A failure-mode and step-budget analysis: VDR is limited by answer verification, not search turns. We defer a full discussion of related work to Appendix A . 2 Setup and Method LiteSearch-VL has three stages, described below after the agent formalism; Figure 2 (Appendix B ) gives an overview of the full pipeline. Agent loop. Given an image I 0 I_{0} and a question q q , a multimodal search agent produces interleaved reasoning, tool-use, and observation steps culminating in a final answer. At step ℓ \ell the policy π θ \pi_{\theta} conditions on the history h ℓ = ( ℐ ℓ , q , 𝐚 < ℓ , 𝐨 < ℓ ) h_{\ell}=(\mathcal{I}_{\ell},q,\mathbf{a}_{<\ell},\mathbf{o}_{<\ell}) , with ℐ ℓ \mathcal{I}_{\ell} the growing visual context, and emits an action a ℓ = [ z ℓ , c ℓ ] a_{\ell}=[z_{\ell},c_{\ell}] : a chain-of-thought z ℓ z_{\ell} plus either a tool call c ℓ ∈ 𝒯 c_{\ell}\in\mathcal{T} or a final response, after which the deterministic environment ℰ \mathcal{E} returns an observation o ℓ = ℰ ⁡ ( c ℓ , h ℓ ) o_{\ell}=\mathcal{E}(c_{\ell},h_{\ell}) that is appended to the history. A rollout terminates when the agent emits a <response> block or the step budget is reached. For a teacher trajectory τ = ( h 0 , a 0 , o 0 ) , … , ( h L , a L ) \tau=(h_{0},a_{0},o_{0}),\dots,(h_{L},a_{L}) the standard supervised fine-tuning objective factors as ℒ SFT ( θ ) = − ∑ ℓ = 0 L [ log P θ ( z ℓ ∣ h ℓ ) + log P θ ( c ℓ ∣ h ℓ , z ℓ ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}(\theta)=-\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\left[\log P_{\theta}(z_{\ell}\mid h_{\ell})+\log P_{\theta}(c_{\ell}\mid h_{\ell},z_{\ell})\right], (1) with observation tokens masked from the loss, and for preference learning at a single step we follow DPO [ 6 ] : ℒ DPO ​ ( θ ) = − 𝔼 ( h , a + , a − ) ​ log ⁡ σ ⁡ ( β ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( a + ∣ h ) π ref ​ ( a + ∣ h ) − β ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( a − ∣ h ) π ref ​ ( a − ∣ h ) ) , \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(h,a^{+},a^{-})}\log\sigma\!\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a^{+}\mid h)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(a^{+}\mid h)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a^{-}\mid h)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(a^{-}\mid h)}\right), (2) where a + a^{+} is the teacher action and a − a^{-} is a synthetic hard negative produced in Stage C. Tool environment. We faithfully re-implement the seven-tool environment of OpenSearch-VL, matching its prompt format, tool schema, and observation tokenization; Table 9 in Appendix F lists every tool and backend. Retrieval tools are backed by SerpAPI [ 7 ] ; the visual-restoration and cropping tools are implemented in Pillow and OpenCV, and OCR uses docTR [ 8 ] . The dispatcher maintains an img_N registry so that visual outputs of one tool can be referenced by index in subsequent calls, and every observation is wrapped in <observation>...</observation> matching the training-time tokenization exactly (required for stable inference). Stage A: supervised distillation from released trajectories. We download the 7-domain SearchVL-SFT-36k corpus (per-domain statistics: Table 3 , Appendix B ) and apply three preprocessing passes: compression strips the upstream chain-of-thought from tool observations and caps each cleaned observation at 4,000 characters, preserving the vast majority of observations end-to-end while removing roughly one third of total tokens; a deterministic per-trajectory hash produces a stratified 36,092 / 500 train / validation holdout split with all seven domains represented in both sides; and step expansion turns each L L -turn trajectory into L L prefix → \to next-step records, yielding 133,439 step-level examples (a 3.65 × \times expansion). We fine-tune Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B on Eq. ( 1 ) with LoRA adapters (rank r = 16 r=16 , α = 32 \alpha=32 ) on the language tower, on a single eight-GPU node with mixed-precision DeepSpeed [ 9 ] ZeRO-3; the 8,192-token cutoff covers the full trajectory distribution at our observation cap, and one epoch over the 36,092 train trajectories at effective batch size 64 corresponds to 564 optimizer steps ( 2B SFT , 4B SFT ). For a controlled comparison, 2B/4B Step-SFT instead train on the prefix → \to next-step expansion, capped to the same optimizer steps and effective batch size with all other hyperparameters identical, isolating the supervision unit from data quantity and optimization budget. Stage B: tool-distilled SFT. Because the full seven-tool action space includes specialized image-restoration and OCR tools that are rarely invoked in the training distribution, we build a distilled variant in which the assistant may only call image_search , text_search , and crop : we rewrite the system prompt and tool schema to be substantially more compact, simplify the text_search argument set, and drop any trajectory (from the full 36,592-record corpus, train and validation combined) that used a disallowed tool, which removes 2,849 records (7.8%) and leaves 33,743. Re-running the same deterministic per-domain stratified split on this filtered pool, targeting a fixed validation size of 500 for direct comparability with Stage A, yields 33,243 train and 500 validation trajectories; this fresh stratified validation sample overlaps the Stage A validation set on 450 records (50 of the original 500 are dropped by the tool whitelist and replaced by surviving records). Everything else (LoRA rank, optimizer, batch size) matches Stage A except for a shorter 6,144-token cutoff enabled by the compact prompt (Table 8 ), so the effective difference is the action space and prompt surface ( 2B/4B 3-tool SFT ). Stage C: synthetic step-level preference optimization. Real on-policy rollouts at training time would dominate the budget; instead we exploit the ∼ \sim 133K teacher decisions the preprocessed step-level corpus already provides. For each step we ask GPT-5 to synthesize hard negatives that a competent but imperfect small VLM would plausibly emit at that decision point, conditioned on the image and the prior history, partitioned into five interpretable failure modes: premature answer (a <response> before sufficient evidence), wrong tool (structurally inappropriate for the next step), weak query (right tool, unfocused or degenerate query), repeated query (duplicates a search already in context), and ignored image (ignores salient evidence in the registered img_N images).
